title: From Gentlemen to Frontiermen: Masculine Formations in English-Language Fiction (1771--1930)
subcategory: digital humanities: structural topic model with covariates
task: Measuring change in masculine character scripts in nineteenth-century fiction
problem: Topic models of whole novels conflate masculine discourse with everything else; seeded vocabularies bias the result.
architecture: BookNLP coreference groups character mentions and infers gender; novels are split into about 500-word windows and male-referent windows are kept; a Structural Topic Model (STM) is fitted with publication year and author gender as topic-prevalence covariates; character names removed by a data-driven document-specificity rule; K = 12 chosen on interpretive grounds after diagnostics for K = 2-15.
llm_or_encoder: none (STM on bag-of-words); BookNLP for coreference

datasets.name: Novel450
datasets.details: txtLAB English subset: 150 British and American novels, 1771-1930 (108 British, 42 American; 81 male-, 69 female-authored); 22,197 male-referent windows out of 35,434

key_results: Six masculine formations recovered without seed words: aristocratic-chivalric, Christian manhood, gentlemanly respectability, country squire, professional-commercial and imperial/adventure.
Formations of inherited rank and sacred authority decline while paid-work and adventure formations rise; imperial/adventure shows the largest increase.
strengths: Character-level text selection makes topics interpretable as masculine scripts.
Covariate modelling (year, author gender) and robustness checks across topic numbers.

limitations.text: Female-dominant passages are excluded, so relational masculinities (fatherhood, courtship) are less visible.
No single K optimises all diagnostics; K = 12 is chosen for interpretability.

notes: Application study from the author-curated corpus.
